items.title: GLM-5.3 Optimizations, Part 2: PCP, DCP, and Hybrid HiSparse on 16 H200s
items.headline: vLLM combines prefill and decode context parallelism with HiSparse KV offload to serve GLM-5.3 at 1M context on 16 H200s
items.summary: Systems write-up (23 Oct) on long-context serving of GLM-5.3 with prefill/decode disaggregation on two 8xH200 nodes. Prefill Context Parallelism (PCP) splits each prompt by token across GPUs (16 chunks paired front-to-back for load balance) and all-gathers new KV so every query sees the full context. Decode Context Parallelism (DCP) shards the KV cache round-robin by token, sends queries to the shards and merges partial attention results. In the prefill engine they run together (PCP8 x DCP8 x EP8, 'PCP splits queries; DCP splits KV') on Model Runner V2, with NIXL reassembling the KV layout for the decode node, which runs 8 DP ranks with EP8 and Hybrid HiSparse host-memory KV (from Part 1). FP8 KV cache, MTP speculative decoding with 3 draft tokens; needs vLLM >= 0.32.0.
items.result: A 1M-token request needs 53.4 GiB of FP8 KV; DCP8 cuts that to about 6.7 GiB per GPU. Sparse-MLA arithmetic intensity rises from ~26 FLOPs/byte (TP8) to ~191 (PCP8; H200 BF16 ridge ~206). DCP overhead is ~6% per step up to 64K cached context and 15% at 248K. On the AgentX benchmark, PCP8xDCP8 prefill gives 1.7-3.2x per-user interactivity at equal throughput versus DP8 prefill (up to c32), and median TTFT drops from 1.5-5.2 s to 0.8-0.9 s. At c64 with HiSparse decode: 8,340 logical tok/s per GPU at 29.6 tok/s per user, while other configurations fall to 1-2 tok/s per user. Only this configuration could serve a 1M-token request.
items.critique: Vendor-team benchmark on one model, one prefill node and one decode node; multi-node scaling and other hardware are untested. MTP acceptance length was fixed at a synthetic 2.99 in every configuration, so real speculative-decoding behaviour is not measured. Throughput counts logical tokens including prefix-cached input, which inflates tok/s. The 1.7-3.2x range is not broken down by context length, 1M-context results cover only c8-c32, and the DCP all-gather is not yet overlapped with compute. Results come from a vLLM main commit, not a release.

items.title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16
items.headline: AMD's ALTO recipe trains GPT-OSS-20B in MXFP4 to within ~0.007 validation loss of BF16 on the MLPerf small-MoE benchmark
items.summary: ALTO is an open-source MXFP4 training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark (C4, Llama-3.1 tokenizer, target validation loss 3.34). All Linear and GroupedExperts layers run in MXFP4 (E2M1 elements, UE8M0 scales); the lm_head and router gates stay unquantized. Activations use 1D 32-element blocks; weights use 2D 32x32 blocks so one quantized copy serves forward and backward. A randomized 32x32 Hadamard transform is applied on the weight-gradient path, gradients use stochastic rounding, and a new optimizer-level de-oscillation hook (adapted from TetraJet-v2) tracks per-element travel over 200 steps and snaps oscillating weights to bin centers after step 2,000.
items.result: Validation loss at 16,128 steps: BF16 3.3283, MXFP4 without de-oscillation 3.3418, full ALTO recipe 3.3350, closing about half the remaining gap. De-oscillation cuts the extra steps needed to reach the 3.34 target from +20.0% to +5.0% versus BF16. Differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping and macro-block scaling improved operator-level SNR but did not help end-to-end.
items.critique: FP4 is simulated (quantize-dequantize, then a high-precision GEMM) on MI300, so there are no speed or memory numbers and the paper says wall-clock was not optimized. One model, one benchmark, a short run (about 2.1B tokens by the summary's estimate of 16,128 steps x 16 x 8,192; token count is not stated in the paper), and only validation loss, with no downstream evaluations. The MLPerf submission is described as incomplete, and much of the recipe is borrowed from prior work.

items.title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
items.headline: Accordion: one 6B-total, 0.5B-active MoE serves five inference budgets by looping a fixed prefix of layers
items.summary: Aims to replace a family of separately trained models with one looped MoE that exposes several compute budgets. Accordion supports five inference budgets via fixed-prefix layer looping: each budget follows a predefined execution path, and the smallest budget is the unlooped model. Pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and uses plain next-token loss with no cross-budget consistency objective. SFT and RL keep all budgets working, and three domain experts are combined into one model through parameter-group merging plus budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
items.result: After 3.6T pretraining tokens, Accordion-6B-A0.5B gains 3.01 points on a five-category macro-average over 37 tasks as depth increases from the smallest to the largest budget; the middle budget captures 89% of that gain with half the additional layer executions. The merged model beats each domain expert on its own task-and-budget average (abstract-level claim).
items.critique: Rests on the abstract: the HTML could not be read, so comparisons with separately trained fixed-depth models of matched compute, or with other elastic-depth or looped methods, are not verified. The headline gain (+3.01 points from extra depth) is modest, and wall-clock latency and KV-cache cost of the looped budgets are not given in the abstract. Only one scale (0.5B active) is reported.

items.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
items.headline: BiLoCo stores FP4 low-rank error corrections as ±1 sign vectors, run on CUDA cores beside the tensor-core GEMM on B300
items.summary: FP4 post-training quantization still leaves an accuracy gap. SVDQuant-style fixes add a high-precision low-rank correction, which costs many bits per rank and competes for the same tensor cores. BiLoCo stores the left and right correction factors as binary {±1} vectors instead of BF16, cutting storage per rank-one component 16x, so the correction becomes additions and subtractions. A fused B300 kernel runs the FP4 GEMM on tensor cores and the bit-packed correction on CUDA cores in the same launch, combining them in the GEMM epilogue. Code (MIT) is on GitHub at jindavid/BiLoCo.
items.result: On 4B-72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or beats memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ (abstract; no numbers given there). The fused kernel is at most 11% slower than the FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for every rank up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 for batch sizes up to 8.
items.critique: Rests on the abstract and the repo README: the HTML could not be read, so per-model perplexity or accuracy numbers, and comparisons with GPTQ-style FP4 methods beyond SVDQuant, are unverified here. The kernel is a slowdown relative to plain FP4, not a speedup, and targets decode batches of at most 32 on Blackwell (sm_103a/100a) only. Neither the abstract nor the README reports end-to-end tokens/s.

items.title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
items.headline: ProQuant prunes MoE experts jointly with bit allocation; Qwen3-30B-A3B averages 67.30 at 1.5 bits/expert vs ≤30.75 for baselines
items.summary: Weight-only mixed-precision PTQ for MoE LLMs at 1.5-2.5 average bits per expert. PoP jointly decides expert pruning and bit widths (candidates {0, 2, 3} bits, 0 = pruned), so a few higher-precision experts replace badly degraded ones, and it accounts for how quantization error propagates across layers. RoCo applies mathematically equivalent transforms to expert inputs (with inverse router scaling) to offset quantization error without fine-tuning the router directly, reducing routing drift. Attention projections are 4-bit, routers full precision; calibration is 128 x 2,048-token C4 sequences.
items.result: At 1.5 average bits, the six-benchmark average on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 is 67.30 (BF16 80.94) versus 24.69 MxMoE, 30.75 GEMQ and 22.09 PMQ; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B it is 60.85 (BF16 87.32) versus 41.42 / 34.73 / 28.08. At 2.0 bits on Qwen3-30B: ProQuant 74.49 versus GPTQ 68.64, GEMQ 50.42, MxMoE 49.89, PMQ 49.65.
items.critique: Only two MoE models, both Qwen-family at ~3B active. Large task-level drops remain at 1.5 bits (Qwen3.5-35B MATH-500 40.20 vs 93.60 BF16). GPTQ is missing at 1.5 bits, ablations for PoP and RoCo were not read, and there are no latency or throughput results; pruning experts changes the model and mixed 2/3-bit experts need kernel support that is not evaluated. Calibration uses C4 only.

items.title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
items.headline: UlaCache gives sparse-attention serving one logical KV address space over GPU pools and CPU memory, up to 2.51x decode throughput
items.summary: Sparse attention selects a subset of past tokens per step, but the full KV cache must stay reachable for later steps. UlaCache puts GPU KV pools and optional CPU memory into one unified logical address space; local GPU buffers keep selected KV entries across decoding steps so only missing entries are transferred, and both data-parallel and tensor-parallel attention are supported. With CPU storage enabled, Parallel Bucketed LRU (PB-LRU) manages a GPU pool shared across requests, updating recency and choosing eviction victims in parallel.
items.result: With speculative decoding on and matched CPU/GPU memory budgets, peak decode throughput versus the state-of-the-art baseline is 1.16x (DP) and 1.70x (TP) on H200, and 1.73x (DP) and 2.51x (TP) on B300.
items.critique: Rests on the abstract: the baseline system, the models, the sparse-attention method and the workloads are not named there, and accuracy is not discussed. Gains are peak throughput with speculative decoding enabled, so latency, tail behaviour and gains without speculative decoding are unknown. The DP gain on H200 is small (1.16x).

items.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.headline: Matching where the trainer rounds to BF16 in RoPE, SwiGLU and RMSNorm to the inference engine prevents RL collapse on Qwen models
items.summary: LLM RL usually uses separate inference and training stacks; even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences turn intended on-policy updates off-policy and can destabilize training. The authors align training-side rounding locations to the inference engine in three regions (RoPE, SwiGLU and residual RMSNorm) by keeping selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. The inference engine, matmul and attention kernels and the objective are unchanged.
items.result: Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse seen with the default BF16 baseline; aligning only the RoPE path also sufficed in the studied runs despite remaining numerical discrepancies (abstract; no quantitative metrics given there).
items.critique: Rests on the abstract, which reports no numbers. Qwen-family only, so other architectures and inference engines are untested. The extra FP32 intermediates cost compute and memory, which the abstract does not quantify. There is no comparison with importance-sampling corrections such as truncated IS, a common fix for training-inference mismatch.

items.title: Speculative Acceptance Does Not Decay with Position: A Full-Length Diagnostic on Long Chain-of-Thought with Independent Drafts
items.headline: Over 1.78M verification rounds on MATH-500, speculative-decoding acceptance does not fall with position in long chain-of-thought
items.summary: Tests the common claim that speculative-decoding acceptance falls as chain-of-thought gets longer, a claim that drives position-aware drafter training. Two independent drafts (same-family DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and cross-family Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) are measured against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B across full generations on all 500 MATH-500 problems, under greedy (0-8K tokens) and sampling (0-12K) decoding, using within-problem paired tests.
items.result: After removing a greedy-decoding repetition pathology, acceptance does not decline with position in any of the four configurations; the second half of trajectories is slightly but significantly higher than the first. A temperature sweep attributes the apparent drop on high-entropy reflection tokens to the argmax-agreement metric. Rejections cluster on reflection words ('wait', 'however', 'check'), and a three-arm LoRA trajectory-alignment intervention did not improve mean accepted length.
items.critique: Single-author diagnostic at small scale (7B target, 1.5B drafts) on one math benchmark; it uses independent draft models rather than EAGLE/MTP-style heads trained on the target's features, which is where the decay claim is usually made. The abstract gives no absolute acceptance rates or speedups.

items.title: Revisiting the 16× Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
items.headline: Re-run of the diffusion-vs-autoregressive scaling study puts the compute gap at 3-8x under current practice, not 16x
items.summary: Re-examines the widely cited result that diffusion LMs need ~16x the pretraining compute of autoregressive models. The authors redo the SMDM scaling-law protocol with three updates: exact likelihood (DUEL) instead of the ELBO, block diffusion (block sizes 4-32), and an encoder-decoder block-diffusion architecture (E2D2). About 1,700 models across ten variants and five budgets from 6e18 to 1e20 FLOPs. The paper is arXiv 2610.17590 (mid-October); this item uses the project page.
items.result: Compute multiple versus AR to match loss: ELBO reproduction 17.8x (prior work reported 16x), exact likelihood 12.8x, block diffusion b=32 9.6x, E2D2 b=32 7.8x, b=16 6.3x, b=8 4.6x, b=4 3.0x. The fitted gap held at a held-out 3e20 FLOP budget, and mean accuracy on eight zero-shot benchmarks ordered variants the same way as likelihood.
items.critique: Small-model regime (≤3e20 FLOPs); single seed, one shared LR/batch configuration, and DUEL measured only with a top-1 confidence sampler. Smaller block sizes move block diffusion toward autoregressive decoding, so the narrower gap partly trades away diffusion's parallel-generation advantage; inference cost is not part of the comparison. Not covered earlier; included as an older paper.

items.title: Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra
items.headline: OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Terra for ChatGPT, Codex and the API at $1/$5 per M input/output tokens, 50% below GPT-5.6 Terra
items.summary: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Terra (26 Oct per coverage), a fast computer-use model, to ChatGPT Plus/Pro/Enterprise/Edu, Codex and the API as gpt-6.1-terra. API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 cached input and $5 output, which OpenAI says is 50% lower than GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol. OpenAI claims it finishes Agents' Last Exam tasks over 3x faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and at max effort is over 3x as token-efficient as Claude Opus 5.5 at a quarter of the per-token price (~9x lower cost per task).
items.result: OpenAI-reported: Terminal-Bench 4.0 50.3% at max effort (GPT-5.6 Terra 21.5%); Agents' Last Exam at medium effort 15 points above GPT-5.6 Terra and on par with GPT-6 Astra at one-tenth its per-token price; error rate on error-inducing factuality prompts down from 53.6% to 16.7% at low effort.
items.critique: All numbers are vendor-reported and not independently verified; speed claims are relative with no absolute latencies. No architecture, parameter count or efficiency technique is disclosed, so it offers nothing technical on the 3x speed and token efficiency. Off focus; included as a major release with pricing and inference-cost implications.
